rubric.why: The starting ion must have a +2 charge to balance the equation.
rubric.description: Identifies the reactant as Fe²⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Fe²⁺ as the reactant.

rubric.why: The equation shows the loss of one electron as Fe²⁺ becomes Fe³⁺.
rubric.description: Shows the one-electron oxidation correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for retaining Fe³⁺ and 1e⁻ on the product side.

modelAnswer: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + 1e⁻

items.followUp: Write down one difference between halogens and noble gases.

rubric.why: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell.
rubric.description: States the outer-shell electron count of alkali metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an alkali metal has one valence electron.

rubric.why: Alkaline earth metals have two electrons in their outermost shell.
rubric.description: Contrasts the outer-shell electron count of alkaline earth metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an alkaline earth metal has two valence electrons.

modelAnswer: An alkali metal has one electron in its outermost shell, whereas an alkaline earth metal has two electrons in its outermost shell.

items.followUp: Why is hydrochloric acid a strong acid in water?

rubric.why: A weak acid ionizes only to a limited extent in water.
rubric.description: States that HF ionizes only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the ionization as partial or incomplete.

rubric.why: Partial ionization produces relatively few hydrogen ions compared with a strong acid of the same concentration.
rubric.description: Explains the low production of hydrogen ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking partial ionization to a low number or concentration of H⁺ ions.

modelAnswer: HF is a weak acid because it ionizes only partially in water.
Consequently, it produces relatively few H⁺ ions.

items.followUp: Define an atom and describe four types of molecules classified by the number of atoms they contain.

rubric.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently while retaining its properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the smallest independently existing particle that retains the substance’s properties.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule consists of one atom.
rubric.description: Describes a monoatomic molecule with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying one atom per molecule; an example such as He may be given.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule consists of two atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a diatomic molecule with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying two atoms per molecule; an example such as H₂ or O₂ may be given.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule consists of three atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a triatomic molecule with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying three atoms per molecule; an example such as H₂O or CO₂ may be given.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a polyatomic molecule with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying more than three atoms per molecule; an example such as P₄ or S₈ may be given.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain the chemical properties of that substance.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom, for example, He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms, for example, H₂.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms, for example, H₂O.
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms, for example, P₄.

items.followUp: Define a covalent bond and explain its formation in a hydrogen molecule.

rubric.why: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: In sodium chloride, sodium transfers one electron to chlorine.
rubric.description: Describes electron transfer in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium donates one electron to chlorine.

rubric.why: The resulting oppositely charged ions attract and form an ionic bond.
rubric.description: Identifies the ions formed and their attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forming an ionic bond through attraction.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
In sodium chloride, a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other, forming an ionic bond in NaCl.

items.followUp: Describe four differences between Thomson’s atomic model and Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model places positive charge in a small nucleus, unlike the spread-out positive charge in the comparison with earlier models.
rubric.description: Contrasts where positive charge is located.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that positive charge is concentrated in the nucleus rather than spread throughout the atom.

rubric.why: Rutherford proposed a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.description: Identifies Rutherford’s nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: States Bohr’s fixed-orbit concept.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying fixed energy levels or stationary orbits.

rubric.why: Electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: Explains the energy behaviour in Bohr’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not radiate energy while in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: Bohr explained spectral lines by electrons emitting or absorbing energy when they change energy levels.
rubric.description: Describes energy changes between Bohr’s levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transitions between energy levels with emission or absorption of energy.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus; Bohr also accepted a central nucleus but added fixed electron energy levels.
In Rutherford’s model, electrons could revolve at various distances; in Bohr’s model, they occupy definite orbits or shells.
Rutherford’s revolving electrons should continuously radiate energy; electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr’s fixed energy levels explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen; Bohr explained it through emission or absorption of energy when electrons change energy levels.

items.followUp: Explain how the vapour pressure of a liquid changes when its intermolecular forces become stronger and when its temperature rises.

rubric.why: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces allow more particles to escape, giving them a higher vapour pressure; stronger forces have the opposite effect.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of the liquid’s nature.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for relating stronger intermolecular forces to lower vapour pressure, or weaker forces/greater volatility to higher vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Heating increases particles’ kinetic energy, so more can escape into the vapour phase and the vapour pressure rises.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that vapour pressure rises with temperature and 1 mark for linking this to more particles escaping or greater kinetic energy.

modelAnswer: The vapour pressure depends on the nature of the liquid: weaker intermolecular forces allow more molecules to escape, so the vapour pressure is higher.
Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have lower vapour pressure.
As temperature increases, the molecules gain kinetic energy and more escape into the vapour phase.
Therefore, vapour pressure increases as temperature rises.

items.followUp: Write down four characteristics of a suspension.

rubric.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: States that a solution is homogeneous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a solution as homogeneous or uniform throughout.

rubric.why: A solution contains a solute dissolved in a solvent.
rubric.description: Identifies the components of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the solute and solvent as its components.

rubric.why: Solution particles are extremely small and cannot be seen individually.
rubric.description: Describes the small size of solution particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are very small or not individually visible.

rubric.why: Solution particles remain dispersed and pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.description: States a characteristic of solution stability or filtration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles do not settle or cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.
It consists of a solute dissolved in a solvent.
Its particles are extremely small and cannot be seen individually.
The particles do not settle and cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.
